definition: A program that reads the commands you type and runs them; on the lab server it is bash.
A window where you type commands to a shell, on your laptop or on the server (in JupyterLab: File → New → Terminal).
A secure way to log in to another computer over the network and run commands there.
A forwarded port that lets the browser on your laptop reach a program on the server (here JupyterLab) through your SSH connection.
A shared computer that many people log in to and run programs on at the same time.
Logging in with your password plus a one-time code from your phone, so a stolen password alone is not enough.
A folder whose full history of changes is tracked by git.
A version-control program that records snapshots of your files so you can compare and undo changes.
One saved snapshot of changes in a git repository, with a short message that says what changed and why.
A named line of commits that lets you work on a change without disturbing the main line.
A GitHub page that proposes merging one branch into another, so someone can review the change first.
The original repository your copy came from; you pull tutorial updates from it.
Your own private GitHub repository that keeps the tutorial's history and holds your work.
The program behind a Jupyter notebook that runs your code cells; in this tutorial it is "SGTL (Python 3.12)".
A self-contained set of Python and packages with fixed versions, so results do not change when other software changes.
A package manager that installs Python and scientific libraries into separate environments.
A program that runs in your web browser and lets you write and run notebooks.
A file (.ipynb) that mixes code, results, figures and text in cells.
One stream of work inside a running program; more threads use more CPU cores at the same time.
One processing unit of a computer; all users of a shared server share a fixed number of them.
The fast working storage that a running program uses; when the server runs out, programs are killed.
Running a script so that it only prints what it would do, without changing anything.
A short written guess of a result, made before you run the code, so you can learn from the difference.
A test that runs your function on cases with known answers and prints PASS or FAIL without showing the solution.
The folder your shell is in right now; pwd prints it, and relative paths start from it.
Your own top folder on the server, written ~ in the shell; your files and the course software live under it.
The address of a file or folder; an absolute path starts at the top folder /, a relative path starts from the working directory.
A number that picks out one program listening for network connections on a computer; JupyterLab listens on one port, and the SSH tunnel forwards it to your laptop.
A named link from your repository to another copy of it, usually on GitHub, that git can push to and pull from; origin and upstream are the two remotes in this course.
Sending the commits you made on your computer to a remote, for example your private copy on GitHub.
Fetching new commits from a remote and merging them into the copy on your computer.
A plain-text table with one row per line and commas between the columns; the earthquake catalogs in this course are CSV files.
The | sign in the shell, which feeds the output of one command into the next command.
Basic Linear Algebra Subprograms: the fast library behind NumPy's matrix and vector arithmetic; it can start many threads unless it is told to use one.
A set of threads that a library starts once and reuses for parallel work; on the shared server each pool is capped at one thread.
The code of 40 letters and digits (often shortened to the first 7) that names one commit exactly.
A way to format plain text with a few marks, such as # for a heading and **bold** for bold text; notebook text cells and these docs use it.
Your record of AI help, one Markdown file per module in work/ai_log/ (for example work/ai_log/M01.md), with an entry every time AI help shaped your work.
A command that runs a program at a lower priority, so that it gives way to other people's work on the shared server.
A pandas table with named columns, like a spreadsheet inside Python.
A named block of code that takes inputs (arguments) and returns an output.
Doing a calculation on a whole array at once instead of looping over the items one by one.
A number that fixes a random-number generator, so the same "random" values come out every time.
The shortest distance between two points measured along the surface of the Earth.
The error report Python prints when a line fails; the last line names the error, and the lines above show where it happened.
A region that keeps one clock time, given as an offset from UTC (KST is UTC + 9 h); Python's zoneinfo module finds named zones such as 'Asia/Seoul' in a time-zone database.
Setting clocks one hour ahead for the summer months, so that in those months the clock's offset from UTC is one hour larger.
An invisible marker that some programs write at the very start of a UTF-8 text file; a program that does not expect it reads it as part of the first value.
A special floating-point value meaning 'not a number'; pandas uses it to mark a missing value.
An array of True and False values, one per element or row, that says where a condition holds.
NumPy's rule for combining arrays of different shapes, for example one number with a whole array, without writing a loop.
The text in triple quotes just below a def line that says what a function does, what it takes and what it returns; help() prints it.
A Python string written with f before the opening quote, in which names in curly braces are replaced by their values.

korean: 나이브 시각, 시간대 정보가 없는 시각
definition: A date and time with no time zone attached, so Python cannot tell which instant on Earth it means.

korean: 인식 시각, 시간대 정보가 있는 시각
definition: A date and time with its time zone attached, so it names one exact instant.
The angle unit that NumPy's trigonometric functions use; a full circle is 2π radians, so 180° is π radians.
The angle at the Earth's center between the lines to two points on its surface.
One column of a pandas table: a list of values with a label (index) for each.
The row labels of a pandas DataFrame or Series; they stay attached to the rows when you select or sort them.
A rule that flattens the curved surface of the Earth onto a flat map.
In Matplotlib the figure is the whole image, and an axes is one plotting panel inside it with its own x and y axes.
A bar chart of how many values fall into each bin (interval), for example how many earthquakes have magnitudes in each 0.1-wide bin.
A plot with one marker per item at its x and y position, for example one dot per earthquake.
Writing labels and titles like a sentence: only the first word and proper names start with a capital letter, as in 'Depth (km)'.
A bar on a map that shows how long a given distance, such as 50 km, is on the map.
The longitude and latitude limits (west, east, south, north) of the area a map shows.
Latitude and longitude written as one decimal number, such as 35.85°, instead of degrees, minutes and seconds.
A plot of each earthquake's magnitude against its origin time, one marker per event.
A table of earthquakes with origin time, location, depth and magnitude, made by a seismological agency.
The earthquakes that occur in a region over a period of time.
The point inside the Earth where an earthquake rupture starts.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the hypocenter.
The time when the earthquake rupture starts at the hypocenter.
The depth of the hypocenter below the surface, in kilometers.
A number on a logarithmic scale that measures the size of an earthquake; one unit means about ten times larger amplitudes.
A magnitude from the largest amplitudes on nearby seismometers, corrected for distance; the KMA catalog reports ML.
A magnitude computed from the seismic moment; unlike ML it does not saturate for large earthquakes.
Shear modulus times fault area times average slip, in newton-meters; the physical size of an earthquake.
Coordinated Universal Time, the reference clock used for all times in this tutorial.
Korea Standard Time, UTC plus 9 hours; the KMA catalog gives its times in KST.
The International Federation of Digital Seismograph Networks, which also defines standard web services for seismic data.
The U.S. Geological Survey's Comprehensive Catalog of earthquakes, which also lists larger Korean events.
The International Seismological Centre, which combines reports from many agencies into one global bulletin.
The Korea Open Government License that lets anyone reuse public data if they name the source.
The number of earthquakes in each magnitude bin, or at or above each magnitude.
The smallest magnitude above which a catalog records (almost) every earthquake in a region and period.
The rounding step of the magnitudes in a catalog, 0.1 for KMA ML; estimators must take it into account.
The rule that the number of earthquakes at or above magnitude M falls by about ten times per magnitude unit: log10 N = a - bM.
The slope of the Gutenberg-Richter law; it is close to 1 in most regions.
The productivity term of the Gutenberg-Richter law: log10 of the number of events at or above magnitude 0.
Choosing the model parameters that make the observed data most probable.
Events that happen at random times, independently of each other, at an average rate (events per unit of time) that can stay the same or change with time, as it falls after a mainshock.
The largest earthquake of a sequence.
An earthquake that comes before a larger earthquake nearby.
An earthquake that follows a larger earthquake nearby and belongs to its sequence.
A group of earthquakes that are close in space and time and are thought to be related.
A sequence without one clearly largest event, often lasting days to months.
The rule that the aftershock rate decays with time t after the mainshock as K/(t + c)^p.
Removing aftershocks and other dependent events so that the remaining events behave like independent background earthquakes.
Earthquakes that were not triggered by earlier earthquakes.
A distance in space, time and magnitude to the most likely parent event (Zaliapin and Ben-Zion), used to separate clusters from background.
The Epidemic-Type Aftershock Sequence model, in which every earthquake can trigger others and the rates add up.
A record of ground motion against time at one station.
An instrument that measures ground motion.
A site with a seismometer, named by a network code and a station code.
A two-letter code for the network a station belongs to, for example KS (KMA) or KG (KIGAM).
One recorded component of a station, named with three letters such as HHZ (band, instrument type, orientation).
The direction of motion a channel records: vertical (Z), north (N) or east (E).
The number of samples recorded per second, in hertz.
Half the sampling rate: the highest frequency a sampled signal can represent.
The raw integer numbers that a digitizer records, before the instrument response is removed.
How the instrument turns ground motion into recorded counts, as a function of frequency.
A compact way to write an instrument response as a ratio of two polynomials.
An XML file format for station locations, channels and instrument responses.
A standard binary file format for waveform data.
Seismogram Transfer Program: a client that fetches waveforms from a data center with your personal account.
Waveform data recorded all the time, as opposed to short windows cut around known events.
The displacement, velocity or acceleration of the ground at a station.
A filter that keeps the frequencies between two corner frequencies and removes the rest.
The amplitude of a signal at each frequency.
The direction from the earthquake to a station, measured clockwise from north.
The direction from a station back toward the earthquake, measured clockwise from north.
Horizontal components rotated to point along (R) and across (T) the direction from the source to the station.
A seismic wave that travels through the inside of the Earth: P or S.
A seismic wave that travels along the Earth's surface; it is slower than body waves and often largest at long distances.
The compressional body wave; it is the fastest wave and arrives first.
The shear body wave; it is slower than P and usually larger on the horizontal components.
The time a seismic phase reaches a station.
A measured arrival time of a seismic phase (P or S) at one station, made by a person or a program.
How much larger the signal is than the background noise.
The ratio of a short-term average to a long-term average of signal amplitude; a sudden rise marks a new arrival.
The moment a detector declares that a signal has started, for example when STA/LTA rises above a threshold.
Whether the first P-wave motion is up (compression) or down (dilatation).
A neural network trained on labeled seismograms to find P and S arrivals, such as PhaseNet.
Grouping picks from many stations into events, so that each pick belongs to one earthquake.
Finding earthquakes in continuous data.
Scanning continuous data with the waveforms of a known earthquake to find similar, often smaller, events.
A measure of how similar two signals are at each relative time shift.
The time a seismic wave takes to travel from the source to a station.
Seismic wave speeds as a function of depth; this tutorial uses layered one-dimensional models.
p = sin(i)/v, which stays constant along a ray in a layered Earth.
The angle between a ray leaving the source and the downward vertical.
The boundary between the crust and the mantle, about 30-35 km deep under South Korea.
A wave that travels along a layer boundary, such as Pn along the Moho; in this tutorial only a travel-time idea, never used for location.
A plot of S-P time against P arrival time; its slope is Vp/Vs minus 1, and the line reaches zero S-P time at the origin time.
The ratio of P-wave speed to S-wave speed; about 1.73 in many crustal rocks.
The delay between the S and P arrivals at a station; it grows with distance from the source.
Locating each earthquake on its own from its arrival times and a velocity model.
An observed value minus the value the model predicts, for example an arrival time.
A single number that measures how badly a model fits the data; location searches for its minimum.
Trying every point on a grid of candidate answers and keeping the best one.
Iterative linearized location: start from a guess, fit the time residuals with small changes, and repeat.
The matrix of partial derivatives of the predicted times with respect to the hypocenter coordinates and origin time.
Choosing the model that makes the sum of squared residuals smallest.
A matrix that describes the uncertainty of estimated parameters and how their errors trade off.
The region where the true epicenter probably lies, drawn from the covariance matrix.
The largest angle between neighboring stations as seen from the epicenter; a large gap means a poorly constrained location.
The root mean square of the travel-time residuals of one event.
A standard USGS program that locates earthquakes in layered velocity models.
The SGTL processing toolchain that runs picking, location, relocation and focal mechanisms in sequence.
Improving the locations of nearby events relative to each other by using differences of travel times.
The difference between the arrival times of the same phase from two events at one station.
The observed minus the predicted differential time of an event pair at one station.
The standard double-difference relocation program (Waldhauser 2001).
Cross-correlation choosing a lag one full period off, because two neighboring peaks look alike.
Adding a penalty that keeps model changes small so an inversion stays stable.
The ratio of the largest to the smallest singular value of a matrix; a large number means an unstable inversion.
Estimating uncertainty by repeating an analysis many times on resampled data.
A fracture in rock along which the two sides have slipped past each other.
The relative movement of the two sides of a fault during an earthquake.
The compass direction of a horizontal line on the fault plane, chosen so that the fault dips to the right.
The angle of the fault plane below the horizontal, from 0 to 90 degrees.
The direction of slip within the fault plane, measured from the strike direction.
A fault on which the two sides slide horizontally past each other (rake near 0 or 180 degrees).
A fault on which the upper side moves down; the crust is extended (rake near -90 degrees).
A fault on which the upper side moves up; the crust is shortened (rake near +90 degrees).
The orientation of the fault and the direction of slip, estimated from seismic waves.
An imaginary small sphere around the hypocenter on which the directions of rays leaving the source are plotted.
Drawing the rays that leave the source downward, as seen from above, on a flat circle.
A printed net for projecting directions on a sphere onto a flat circle by hand.
One of the two planes on which P-wave amplitude is zero; one of them is the fault plane.
The nodal plane that is not the fault plane.
The pressure (P) and tension (T) axes, which lie halfway between the two nodal planes.
The map-view drawing of a focal mechanism, with the compressional quadrants shaded.
How P-wave and S-wave amplitudes vary with direction from the source.
The ratio of S-wave to P-wave amplitude, which adds information to polarities when estimating mechanisms.
A Python program, successor of HASH, that finds focal mechanisms and their uncertainty from polarities and S/P ratios.
The smallest rotation that turns one double-couple mechanism into another; 0 degrees means identical.
A symmetric 3-by-3 matrix that describes the forces of an earthquake treated as a point source.
The moment tensor of slip on a flat fault: two opposite pairs of forces with no net force or torque.
Compensated linear vector dipole: a non-double-couple part of a moment tensor with no volume change.
The volume-change part of a moment tensor, as in an explosion or implosion.
A part of a sphere (Tape and Tape 2012) on which every moment-tensor source type has a place, from explosion to double couple.
Treating an earthquake as happening at one point, which is fine when the wavelengths are much longer than the rupture.
The time history of moment release at the source.
The part of the wavefield that decays as 1/r and dominates far from the source.
The decrease of amplitude with distance because the wave energy spreads over a larger area.
The seismogram that a unit impulse source would produce at a station; synthetics are sums of Green's functions weighted by moment-tensor elements.
A seismogram computed from a source and an Earth model instead of recorded.
A method that computes synthetic seismograms in a layered Earth by summing over wavenumbers; PyFK uses it.
Finding source parameters by fitting synthetic seismograms to recorded ones.
How much of the recorded signal the synthetics explain, in percent.
A small shift allowed between data and synthetics to absorb errors of the velocity model.
Two ways to add up residuals: absolute values (L1, less sensitive to outliers) or squares (L2).
The change in shear stress in the slip direction plus effective friction times the change in normal stress (unclamping positive); a positive value brings a fault closer to failure.
A symmetric 3-by-3 matrix that gives the force per area on any plane through a point.
The stress parallel to a plane, which tends to make the plane slip.
The stress perpendicular to a plane; in Coulomb calculations tension (unclamping) is positive.
The friction coefficient reduced to include pore-pressure changes, often written μ' = μ(1 - B).
The fraction of a change in mean stress that appears as a change in pore-fluid pressure.
The pressure of the fluid in the pores and cracks of rock.
The fault whose slip causes the stress change.
The fault on which the stress change is calculated.
Formulas for the displacement and strain caused by slip on a rectangular fault in an elastic half-space (Okada 1992).
A uniform elastic body that fills everything below a flat free surface.
A rock's resistance to shearing, about 30 GPa in the crust.
The ratio of sideways contraction to lengthwise extension when a material is stretched.
Small daily stress changes caused by the tides of the solid Earth and the oceans.
Checking whether a pattern could arise by chance, for example by randomly rotating the stress field or the aftershocks.
The method behind a magnitude value, such as ML, mb or Mw; for one earthquake, values of different types can differ by several tenths.
A magnitude from the amplitude of the first P waves (period near one second) recorded far away; it stops growing for large earthquakes, near 6.
The standard XML file format for earthquake catalogs; each event can hold several origins and magnitudes with their uncertainties, and depths are in meters.
In KMA usage, an earthquake smaller than ML 2.0.
A period in which a seismic network had about the same stations, so its catalog has about the same completeness.
How computers store decimal numbers: in binary, so most decimals such as 0.1 are stored as a value very close to, but not exactly, that number.
A running total: the number of events up to a given time, or at or above a given magnitude.
A quick estimate of the magnitude of completeness: the magnitude bin with the most events in the non-cumulative FMD, often with 0.2 added.
The moment chosen as t = 0 when the times of a sequence are counted, usually the origin time of the mainshock.
Pairing the rows of two catalogs that describe the same earthquakes, using limits on the differences in origin time and epicenter.
A distribution of positive numbers in which larger values become rarer by a constant factor per unit; magnitudes above Mc follow it with rate beta = b ln 10.
The probability that a random value is at or below a given value.
How probable the observed data are under a model, seen as a function of the model's parameter values.
A systematic error: averaged over many repeats, the estimate differs from the true value.
The typical size of the error of an estimate: how much it would scatter if the experiment could be repeated.
Repeating a calculation on many random data sets to see how much the results scatter.
Taking as Mc the smallest magnitude above which the b-value stops changing by more than its uncertainty.
The temporary loss of small events right after a large earthquake, when its waves and its many aftershocks hide them on the seismograms.
A b-value estimated from the positive magnitude differences between consecutive events, which resists short-term incompleteness (van der Elst 2021).
Minus the natural logarithm of the likelihood; minimizing it gives the same parameters as maximizing the likelihood.
Finding the parameter values that minimize a function by trying values step by step on a computer, for example with scipy.optimize.minimize.
When a change of one model parameter can be compensated by a change of another, so that the data cannot tell them apart well.
Making random draws from a distribution by putting uniform random numbers between 0 and 1 into the inverse of its cumulative distribution function.
The user name and password (or key) that let a program act in your name; never share, paste or commit them.
The rules that say who may read, write or run a file; chmod 600 lets only the owner read and write it.
The short code of one seismic station, such as SAJB or CHS; together with the network code it names one site.
A station that no longer records; its code stays in old data and in full station rosters, but not in a list of today's stations.
The full name of a recorded channel, written NET.STA.LOC.CHA, for example KS.SAJB..HHZ (an empty location code gives two dots in a row).
The part of a SEED id that tells apart two sensors of the same kind at one station; it is often empty.
The first letter of a channel code: the sampling rate and the period range of the sensor (H and E: 80-250 samples per second; B and S: 10-80).
The second letter of a channel code: the kind of sensor (H high-gain seismometer, L low-gain seismometer; G an accelerometer in the KS and KG networks).
A seismometer that records ground velocity faithfully over a wide range of periods, from a fraction of a second to tens of seconds.
A seismometer that records ground velocity well at periods of about one second and shorter.
A sensor that measures ground acceleration and stays on scale in strong shaking.
A waveform file in the format of the Seismic Analysis Code: one channel per file, a header with the station, channel and times, then the samples.
The start and the end of a piece of record, for example from 30 s before to 470 s after an origin time.
A period during which a station or channel kept the same site, instruments and settings; station metadata lists one epoch per change.
The distance from the epicenter to a station along the Earth's surface.
The straight-line distance from the hypocenter (at depth) to a station.
A comparison of the data you asked for with the data you received, made before any analysis.
One step of the recording chain, such as the sensor, the digitizer or a digital filter, with its own gain and units.
How much one response stage multiplies its input at a reference frequency, for example 1500 volts per meter per second.
The device that measures a sensor's voltage many times per second and writes it as whole numbers (counts).
The counts recorded per unit of ground motion (for example counts per m/s) where the response is flat: the product of the gains of all stages.

A channel that records the ground motion upside down. By convention a negative stage gain in the metadata marks it, but metadata can be wrong: the records decide (first motions compared with neighbours at the same azimuth, over several earthquakes).
Dividing a record by the instrument response, frequency by frequency, to turn counts into ground motion.
A smooth taper in frequency used while removing the response, so that frequencies where the response is tiny are not blown up.
The torsion seismograph that Richter used for the local magnitude scale; today its records are simulated from digital data.
A smooth curve that follows the size of the wiggles of a signal, computed as the size of the analytic signal.
One channel's record in ObsPy: the samples in tr.data and their description (station, channel, start time, sampling rate) in tr.stats.
A list of ObsPy Traces, for example the three components of one station, as obspy.read returns them.
The fixed block of numbers and short texts at the start of a SAC file: reference time, sampling interval, picks, station and event positions; -12345 means not set.
The moment written in the nz headers of a SAC file; every other SAC time (b, e, o, a, t0) is a number of seconds after it.
The number of a day counted from 1 January (1) to 31 December (365 or 366); SAC stores dates this way in nzjday.
The false, lower frequency that a wave above the Nyquist frequency takes on when it is sampled too slowly.
Removing the mean or a straight line from a record before filtering or transforming it.
A smooth fade of both ends of a record to zero, so that filters and transforms do not see a jump where the record starts and stops.
A frequency where a filter starts to weaken the signal; a band-pass filter has two.
How steeply a filter weakens the frequencies outside its band; ObsPy calls it the number of corners.
A filter that uses only the present and past samples: nothing appears before an arrival, but waves come out delayed and reshaped.
A filter run forward and then backward: peaks stay in place, but some energy spreads to times before an arrival.
The time by which a filter delays the waves of one frequency.
A method that overwrites the object it is called on instead of returning a changed copy; ObsPy's detrend, taper and filter work this way.
Writing a record as a sum of sines and cosines of different frequencies; numpy.fft computes the discrete version.
A logarithmic measure of an amplitude ratio, 20 log10(A1 / A2): 20 dB is a factor of 10.
A floor, in decibels below the largest value of an instrument response, under which the response may not fall when a record is divided by it.
A figure of many seismograms, each drawn at its distance from the source, against time after the origin.
The largest absolute ground velocity of a record, measured after the instrument response is removed.
A new program started by a running program; it gets only the environment variables that it is handed.
The time the processor cores spent on a program, added over all its threads; CPU time divided by wall-clock time is the number of busy cores.
A short fingerprint computed from every byte of a file, here with SHA-256: if even one byte changes, the fingerprint changes, so an unchanged fingerprint shows that the file is intact.
A control in a notebook, such as a slider or a button, that runs code again when you move it; the course's explorers use widgets to redraw a figure.
A record paired with a copy of itself in which every frequency is shifted by a quarter of a cycle; the size of the pair is the envelope.
A common filter design that passes its band as evenly as possible and fades smoothly outside it; more corners make the fade steeper.
A rule that predicts each sample of a record from the few samples just before it.
A score for comparing models that weighs how well each fits the data against how many numbers it needs; the lower score wins.
The first sample where a new arrival starts to show in a record.
An onset that leaves the noise within a sample or two; it can be timed to a few hundredths of a second.
An onset that grows slowly out of the noise, so that its time is uncertain by a tenth of a second or more.
How far the true arrival time may lie from a pick, in seconds; every pick carries one.
A trace computed from a record, such as its squared samples, whose changes a detector looks for.
The average of the last N samples of a record, computed again at every sample.
The value a ratio must rise above to turn a trigger on (thr_on), or fall back to to turn it off again (thr_off).
A trigger on noise, a spike or anything else than the arrival you are looking for.
What happens when a result is too large for its whole-number type: it wraps around to a wrong value without a warning (32-bit integers hold up to about 2.1 billion).
The sample at which the statistics of a record, such as its variance, change.
The median of the sizes of a set of errors, ignoring their signs; a few very large errors barely move it.
A computer model made of many simple arithmetic steps linked in a chain, whose numbers (weights) are set by training on examples; PhaseNet is one.
The labeled examples a network learns from, for a picker records with analysts' picks; the network also learns the habits of those analysts.
The numbers inside a neural network that training has set; the same network with other weights is a different picker.
A network together with weights that someone already trained on a labeled data set, ready to be run on new records.
Running a trained network on new data to get its output; nothing is learned while it runs.
A deep-learning picker (Zhu and Beroza, 2019) that turns 30 s of a three-component record into P, S and noise probabilities for every sample.
About a million labeled three-component records of earthquakes and noise from many regions, used to train many deep-learning pickers.
A piece of record of fixed length that is moved along the record in steps, so a program that sees only 30 s at a time can cover a long record.
Scaling each piece of record before a network sees it, for example by its largest value or its standard deviation, so that large and small earthquakes give numbers of the same size.
Throwing away a network's output near both ends of each piece of record, where it saw too little record around a sample; it makes probability curves start later and end earlier than the record.
SeisBench's name for the output of a model run on a record: an ObsPy Stream with one probability curve per phase (P, S and noise) for every station.
The output of a deep-learning picker: for every sample a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely it is that a P (or S) wave arrives at that moment.
The smallest pick probability that may become a pick; a lower threshold gives more picks, and more false ones.
A sample of a curve that is higher than both of its neighbours.
A pick where no real arrival is, for example on noise, on a spike, or on another phase.
An error with the same sign and about the same size every time, such as picks that are always a few samples late; averaging more values does not remove it.
The median of the distances of the values from their own median: a measure of scatter that a few wild values cannot pull far.
PocketQuake's name for one set of earthquakes processed together, registered under a short name (its slug); its results go to their own folder.
A network of the PhaseNet family (EQNet) that also gives every P pick a first-motion polarity and an amplitude; PocketQuake uses it through sgtl.
A named setting that a program reads from its environment, such as OMP_NUM_THREADS; a program started from Python inherits the environment of the Python process.
A computation that gives exactly the same output, byte for byte, every time it runs on the same input with the same software and settings.
The wave that leaves the source upward and reaches the station without being reflected, bending only where it crosses a layer boundary.
A layer with no bottom: in a layered model, the deepest layer, which continues downward forever.
At a boundary between two layers, sin(angle from the vertical) divided by the wave speed is the same on both sides; it tells how a ray bends.
One divided by the wave speed, in seconds per kilometre.
Finding the ray that reaches a given station by trial: fire a ray, see where it lands, adjust its ray parameter and fire again.
Finding where a quantity crosses a target value by halving an interval that contains the crossing, again and again.
A seismic ray follows the path along which the travel time is least (more exactly, does not change for small changes of the path).
The angle from the vertical at which a ray meeting a faster layer below is bent to run along the boundary: sin(angle) = slower speed / faster speed.
The shortest epicentral distance at which the head wave along a given boundary arrives.
The epicentral distance beyond which a head wave arrives before the direct wave.
Where the straight travel-time line of a head wave, extended back, meets zero distance; it depends on the layer thicknesses and the source depth.
The P and S head waves that run along the top of the mantle, just below the Moho; never used for location in this course.
Travel time minus distance divided by a fixed speed (t - x / v); it tilts travel-time curves so that small differences show.
A widely used program (also inside ObsPy as obspy.taup) that computes travel times and ray paths in a layered spherical Earth model.
A change of depths and speeds that makes travel times in flat layers equal to those in a spherical Earth, and back.
The wave that reaches a station first, whichever path it took: the direct wave near the source, a head wave beyond a crossover distance; the onset a picker marks.
A text file with one JSON object per line, so that a program can add a record by appending one line.
HYPOINVERSE's output with one line per earthquake: origin time, hypocenter, number of readings, gap, RMS residual and errors.
HYPOINVERSE's output with, for each earthquake, a header line and one line per station holding the residuals and the weights it used.
A text format in which every value sits in fixed character columns instead of being separated by commas or blanks.
A decimal point that is not written in a number but fixed by the format: in the format F4.2 the text 1234 means 12.34.
A number from 0 (full weight) to 4 (no weight) attached to a pick that tells a locator how much to trust it.
Giving readings at distant stations less weight in a location, down to none beyond a chosen distance.
Giving readings with large travel-time residuals less weight, down to none, so that a wrong pick cannot pull a location.
The depth at which an iterative locator starts its search for each earthquake.
HYPOINVERSE's horizontal (ERH) and vertical (ERZ) location errors in km, taken from the error ellipsoid of the final solution.
A letter from A (best) to D that sums up how well a location fits and how well the stations surround it; the numbers behind it say more.
The epicentral distance of the closest station with a reading; a depth is best fixed when a station lies closer than about the depth itself.
A constant time added to the predicted travel time at one station, standing for what the velocity model leaves out near that station.
A pick that labels an arrival with the wrong phase, for example an S wave picked as P.
A record that runs without a break for hours or days, instead of a short piece cut around a known earthquake.
Deciding from records that an earthquake happened, and when, without being told beforehand.
Declaring an event only when several stations trigger at about the same time, so that noise at one station is not taken for an earthquake.
Extra time after an event's triggers have ended during which a trigger at another station still joins the same event.
A short piece of a known earthquake's record on one channel, compared with a long record to find events that look like it.
A number from -1 to 1 that says how alike two equally long pieces of record are in shape, whatever their sizes: 1 for the same shape, 0 for no likeness, -1 for the same shape upside down.
The correlation coefficient of a template with every piece of a longer record of the same length, one value per shift.
A detector that slides a known signal along a record and measures how well each piece fits it; template matching is one.
How much later a wave arrives at one station than at another, because it travels farther or more slowly.
The average of the correlation coefficients of all channels after each is shifted back by its moveout, so that one earthquake lines up on every channel.
The value a detector's output must reach for an event to be declared.
The square root of the mean squared distance of values from their mean: a measure of scatter that a few large values can pull far up.
A declared event that is not an earthquake: noise, a glitch or a chance likeness.
How many false detections a detector makes per hour on records that hold no event.
A template finding its own earthquake; it matches perfectly by construction, so it tests the bookkeeping, not the detector.
Running a method on data in which the effect cannot be present (for example records reversed in time), to see how often it finds something anyway.
A magnitude found by comparing an event's amplitudes with those of a reference event of known magnitude on the same channels.
The size of one record divided by the size of another on the same channel; one magnitude unit is a ratio of 10.
The square root of the sum of the squared samples of a record: its overall size.
A pick time minus the predicted travel time from a source to its station: the origin time that pick points to.
How far apart the back-projected origin times of picks may lie and still belong to one event.
Two earthquakes whose arrival times at the same stations are compared; double-difference relocation works on many such pairs at once.
The program of the HypoDD package that pairs nearby earthquakes and writes their catalog differential times (the file dt.ct) from a phase file.
An observation far outside what the others and the physics allow, usually a mistake such as a pick on another wave; programs remove such values by a rule.

A differential time measured by sliding the waveforms of two earthquakes at one station against each other and taking the shift at which they are most alike; for similar waveforms it is good to about a millisecond.
The time by which one signal is shifted against another; in cross-correlation, the shift at which the two match best.
Measuring a time more finely than the sampling interval, for example to a millisecond from records sampled every 10 ms, by interpolating between samples.
Fitting a parabola through a peak sample and its two neighbors and taking the top of the parabola as the position of the peak between samples.
A short wave shape, a few oscillations long; the Ricker wavelet, the second derivative of a bell curve, is a common test signal.
How much a quantity changes when one of its inputs changes a little and all others stay fixed; here, how a travel time changes when the source moves a little east, north or down.
A ray that runs along the straight line from the source to the station, as it does in a medium with the same speed everywhere.
One of the numbers that say how strongly a matrix stretches the directions of its input; a zero or tiny singular value marks a combination of unknowns that the data cannot resolve.
The changes of the unknowns that do not change the predicted data at all, so that the data cannot decide anything about them.
The mean position of the earthquakes of a cluster.
Least squares with a penalty on the size of the solution (the damping squared times its squared length), which keeps an unstable inversion from making huge changes.
Extra equations that keep the mean change of all events' positions and origin times at zero, so that the cluster as a whole stays where it started.
Writing a matrix as a rotation, a stretching by its singular values and another rotation; HypoDD solves small clusters with it.
An iterative method for large least-squares problems (Paige & Saunders 1982); HypoDD uses it, with damping, for large clusters.
Replacing a curved relation by its straight tangent near the current values, so that a small change can be found by solving linear equations.
Repeating a calculation, each time starting from the result of the round before, until the result stops changing.
A number that says how much one observation counts in a fit; its row of the equations is multiplied by it, so a weight of 0 removes the observation.
A file to which every run of a program adds one line saying what ran, when, whether it worked and which files it wrote; sgtl keeps one in work/.sgtl/runs.jsonl.
The number a program gives back when it ends: 0 means it worked, anything else that it stopped with a problem or never started.
The time at which a file's contents were last written, kept by the file system.
A result file left over from an earlier run that a later run did not replace, for example because that run failed; reading it as the new result is a common mistake.
One rerun of an analysis on a data set drawn with replacement from the original data; the spread of many replicas measures the uncertainty.
The value below which a given percentage of a set of values lies; the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles enclose the middle 95 %.
Distances east and north of a chosen reference point in kilometres, with depth counted down from the surface; used instead of latitude and longitude over a small region.
An approximate derivative: the change of a function over a small step divided by the length of the step.
The square system G^T G m = G^T d whose solution m is the least-squares fit of G m to the data d.
The test that ends an iteration, for example a step shorter than a set length or a largest number of steps.
A trial hypocenter above the Earth's surface, produced by a location step; locators prevent it, for example by halving the depth instead.
Travel times computed once on a grid of distances and depths and interpolated afterwards, so that a locator does not trace rays for every trial point.
Locating an earthquake again with its depth held at each of a series of values, to see how the misfit and the other unknowns change with depth.
A text file that holds the picks of earthquakes in the fixed format that a location program reads.
How strongly the errors of two estimated values go together, from -1 to 1: their covariance divided by the product of their standard errors; near -1 or 1 the data cannot tell the two apart.

The sum of the products of two equally long records divided by the product of their L2 norms: the correlation coefficient without removing their means first, 1 when one record is a positive multiple of the other.
The unit vector perpendicular to the fault plane, pointing from the footwall into the hanging wall.
The unit vector in the fault plane along which the hanging wall moves.
The unit vector along which a seismic ray leaves the source, set by the station's azimuth and the takeoff angle.
A mechanism whose misfit lies within a chosen tolerance of the best one; together they show how well the data fix the mechanism.
A 3-by-3 matrix that turns one set of perpendicular axes into another without stretching them.
A group of acceptable mechanisms that lie close to each other and far from the other acceptable mechanisms.
A grade from A (best) to D that HASH and SKHASH give a mechanism from the spread of its acceptable mechanisms and its misfit.
The stretch of record after a pick in which a program takes the largest amplitude of that phase.
The block of rock above a dipping fault plane.
The block of rock below a dipping fault plane.
The coordinate order of Aki & Richards: x1 points north, x2 east and x3 down.
The coordinate order of the Global CMT catalog and of ObsPy's beachballs: r points up, theta south and phi east.
A vector of length 1, which gives a direction only.
The sum of the products of the matching components of two vectors; it is zero when the vectors are perpendicular.
A vector perpendicular to two given vectors, with a length equal to the area of the parallelogram they span.
The azimuth of a line, clockwise from north, of the end that points down.
The angle of a line below the horizontal, from 0 (horizontal) to 90 degrees (vertical).
The line where the two nodal planes of a mechanism meet; it is perpendicular to the P and T axes.
A way to draw a half sphere on a flat circle that keeps equal areas equal; seismologists draw focal mechanisms on it.
A stereographic way to draw a half sphere on a flat circle; it keeps angles, but crowds the area near the centre.
A P first motion that pushes the ground away from the source; on a vertical sensor it is up (U).
A P first motion that pulls the ground towards the source; on a vertical sensor it is down (D).
A ray that leaves the source upward (takeoff angle above 90 degrees), such as the direct wave to a nearby station.
The direction pointing the other way through the centre of a sphere; an upgoing ray is drawn at its antipode on the lower half.
An older (CGS) unit of seismic moment: 1 N m is 10 million (1e7) dyne-cm. Hanks and Kanamori and PyFK use it.
The two parts of an S wave's motion: SV moves in the vertical plane that holds the ray, SH moves horizontally, across that plane.
The terms of a source's wavefield that decay faster than 1/r (as 1/r^2 and 1/r^4); they matter within a few wavelengths of the source and leave a permanent displacement.
A model of uniform rock that goes on forever in every direction, with no surface or layers; its seismograms have a formula.
The ground surface in a model Earth: the rock above it is air, so waves reflect there and the motion at the surface is amplified.
A separate software environment that a notebook runs as another program (here PyFK's Python 3.9), exchanging only files with it.
The spacing of the horizontal wavenumbers that an FK program sums over; too coarse a step adds false arrivals, and PyFK sets it from the largest distance of a call.
A number that says how little energy a wave loses per cycle in the rock; a large Q means little loss (attenuation).
Adding up sampled values times the time step (a running sum or the trapezoid rule) to turn, for example, a velocity record into displacement.

The whole number that PocketQuake gives an event in the files it writes for HYPOINVERSE, HypoDD and SKHASH; the cuspid column of mechanisms.csv links it to PocketQuake's event_id, and SKHASH's own tables call it event_id.

The set of all orientations that a double couple can take, with the Kagan angle as the distance between two of them; turning a mechanism further and further about one fixed axis moves it along a line in this space.
The force per area acting on one particular plane through a point: the stress tensor times the plane's unit normal.
The average of the three normal stresses, one third of the trace of the stress tensor; it squeezes or stretches a volume without shearing it.
An area where an earthquake lowered the Coulomb failure stress, moving faults there away from failure.
The relative change of length and shape of a piece of rock, without units; the symmetric part of the gradient of the displacement.
The linear rule that turns strain into stress in an elastic material; an isotropic material needs two constants for it (the Lamé parameters).
The two constants of Hooke's law for an isotropic elastic material: lambda and the shear modulus mu, both in Pa.
A corner of the rectangle that represents a fault; some programs place the rectangle by a corner instead of by its centre.
The average drop of shear stress on a fault during an earthquake, in MPa; it links fault size, slip and moment.
A fault model that slips over a disc; Eshelby (1957) relates its moment, radius and stress drop.
An empirical formula, fitted to many earthquakes, that gives rupture length, width, area or slip from the magnitude.
How far an earthquake's true position may lie from its catalog position, in km, including the rounding of the catalog.
A chance model built by turning a cloud of points about a centre by random angles, keeping every distance and depth.
The probability, under a chance model, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed; a small value means chance alone rarely gives it.
A short program that looks at the inputs and the requested resources of a heavy run before the run starts, and stops it when something is wrong.
A code from 0 (full weight) to 4 (no weight) that HYPOINVERSE reads for every arrival in its phase file; PocketQuake sets it from the pick probability or from the station distance.
One row per event with every measured number next to its uncertainty, so that a reader sees at once what is known and how well.
Which stations were recording, and how near and how evenly around a source, when an earthquake happened; it limits what a location or a mechanism can resolve.
A list, made before any download or analysis, of the events, the stations that were running for each of them and the cost of getting the records.
A table that lists each claim of a published study as one checkable sentence, with the value it reports, the test that would check it and the result that would refute it.
A statement that a stated measurement could prove wrong; 'the events are deep' becomes testable only when it says how deep and which result would refute it.
A statement about nature that a planned test can support or reject.
A document, written and frozen before any result is seen, that states the questions, hypotheses, tests and decision rules of a study.
What an analyst has already seen of the data or of published results before writing a plan, and which could shape the choice of tests.
The numbers, written down before the results, that decide whether a test supports or rejects a hypothesis.
A dated change to a frozen analysis plan that says what changed, why, and whether results had been seen before the change.
A dated record of what was run, with which settings, and what came out; entries are added, never deleted.
A 32-character hexadecimal fingerprint of a file's bytes; shorter and older than SHA-256, enough to show that a file has not changed but no protection against forgery.
Writing down and freezing the questions, tests and decision rules of a study before seeing its results, so that the choice of test cannot follow the hoped-for answer.
A moment tensor whose three eigenvalues add up to zero: a source without a change of volume (a double couple, a CLVD or a mix of the two).
The records that a source with one moment-tensor element equal to 1 N m and the other five zero would make; every record of a point source is a sum of six of them.
The sum of squared errors, each divided by its variance (in matrix form e^T C^-1 e); for Gaussian errors its average equals the number of free parameters.
A stretch of samples with no valid record (a dead channel, a missing station), marked NaN; it must leave a fit, not enter it as zeros.
A number lambda for which a matrix times some vector (its eigenvector) equals lambda times that vector; a symmetric 3 x 3 tensor has three, with perpendicular eigenvectors.
MTUQ's misfit that adds, over traces, the square root of each trace's sum of squared residuals: L2 inside a trace, L1 across traces.
One over the sum of the squared shares of a total; it counts how many parts effectively make up the total (K when K parts share it equally, 1 when one part has it all).
Precomputed Green's functions stored by velocity model, source depth and distance, from which a program builds synthetics for any source and station without recomputing them.
Moment Tensor Uncertainty Quantification: an open-source Python package (Thurin et al. 2025) that estimates moment tensors and their uncertainty by grid searches over waveform misfits.
Multiplying each trace by a power of its distance before a fit, so that near stations do not dominate a misfit only because their records are larger.
A test before a fit that compares station amplitudes corrected for distance with their common level, and leaves out a station far off it (a wrong gain, a unit error).
A decision, by rules fixed before a run, whether a result is resolved, provisional or not resolved, from numbers such as n_eff, the spread of acceptable solutions and an independent comparison.
A dated line in an analysis plan in which the mentor, by name, states that the plan and its criteria were read before the freeze; a plan without it is not frozen.
A versioned collection of waveform templates and their source events, channels, picks and processing settings used together in a detection search.
Combining repeated reports of one candidate from several templates while retaining the individual matches and their template identities; this is different from statistical declustering.
Measuring a frozen method on data kept separate from template selection and parameter tuning; data already inspected are not a blind test.
Adding known signals to background records and measuring which are detected under a frozen method; recovery depends on the injected signals and noise conditions.
A systematic difference caused by how examples or observations are selected, such as a template bank favoring events with similar waveforms and station coverage.
A program interface with windows and mouse controls; here SeisComP displays waveforms and event context.
A seismological software package; the tutorial uses its offline scrttv waveform viewer and scolv event picker.
The XML file format used by SeisComP for inventories and event measurements; origin depth is in kilometres unlike QuakeML metres.
An SSH feature that lets a desktop application running on the server display a window on your laptop.
